title: Filming What One Cell Does Next

scenes.tts: A fixed, stained cell is dead. One picture of it cannot say which cell moved, which event came first, or whether a green cell went on to divide. Film answers three questions: in what order, how fast, and what did this particular cell do next.
scenes.visual: Three fixed snapshots of a field of cells with green nuclei; question marks over which cell moved, which came first, and which green cell divides; then a film strip of frames replaces the single picture.
scenes.narration: A fixed, stained cell is dead. One picture of it cannot say which cell moved, which event came first, or whether a green cell went on to divide. Film answers three questions: in what order, how fast, and what did this particular cell do next.

scenes.tts: The cell makes its own label. A protein of interest is tagged with a genetically encoded fluorescent protein. Fluorescence from green fluorescent protein, or G F P, was shown in E coli and in C elegans in 1994. A fluorescence microscope separates the excitation light from the longer-wavelength light the label gives off, so the tagged protein stands out against a dark background.
scenes.visual: A cell with a few green dots; blue excitation light enters a filter, the longer green light leaves; the screen shows green spots on black.
scenes.caption: The cell makes its own label. A protein of interest is tagged with a genetically encoded fluorescent protein. scenes.tts: The living cells or animals sit on the microscope stage, kept alive: cells in a dish, brain slices, a transparent larva, or an anaesthetised animal. The same field is imaged again and again at a chosen interval. Chromosomes in human cells were imaged every 30 seconds. Arabidopsis ovules, every 5 minutes. Brain slices and cultures, every few minutes.
scenes.visual: A dish on a stage under a lens; a clock ticks and a frame is captured each interval, frames stack into a filmstrip; three interval rulers (30 s, 5 min, a few min) with tick marks.

scenes.tts: Then each cell is followed from frame to frame. This is tracking. Its colour, its shape changes and its division are read as one history. Two Foochee reporters can mark the cell cycle. A red nucleus is in G zero or G one. A green nucleus is in S, G two or M.
scenes.visual: Filmstrip frames; one cell is circled in each frame and a line links its positions; the nucleus colour changes red to green along the track; legend chips red = G0 and G1, green = S, G2 and M.
scenes.caption: Then each cell is followed from frame to frame. This is tracking. Its colour, its shape changes and its division are read as one history. Two FUCCI reporters can mark the cell cycle. A red nucleus is in G0 or G1. A green nucleus is in S, G2 or M.
scenes.narration: Then each cell is followed from frame to frame. This is tracking. Its colour, its shape changes and its division are read as one history. Two FUCCI reporters can mark the cell cycle. A red nucleus is in G0 or G1. A green nucleus is in S, G2 or M.

scenes.tts: A movie is read as a sequence. Take the position of each tracked cell in every frame, then measure a rate, distance over time, or an order of events. On a cell cycle movie, red, then green, then a rounded dividing cell, then two dim daughters marks one completed cycle. A green cell alone is not a completed cycle.
scenes.visual: Example data: a distance-versus-time track with slope marked as rate; then a colour-bar lineage of one tracked cell red, green, round, two dim daughters, labelled one completed cycle; a lone green cell labelled only entry into S.

scenes.tts: Imaging itself costs the cell. Illumination damages cellular molecules and can impair physiology or kill the sample, in ways that are not always visible in its shape. Limit illumination, for example to the focal plane, and test for phototoxicity effects. A single frame can also mislead about fate. A lagging chromosome in one frame does not give the daughter's final chromosome count. Follow it until its fate is clear.
scenes.visual: Cell with light cone; a damage gauge fills as frames are taken; control chips limit light to focal plane and test for effects. Then one frame of a dividing cell with a laggard chromosome marked question, the next frames resolve it to a final count.

scenes.tts: In 2001, Noctor, Kriegstein and colleagues labelled a few cells in embryonic rat cortex with a retrovirus carrying a fluorescent protein. Time-lapse images showed that proliferative radial glia generate neurons. A fixed section cannot show who gave birth to whom. In 2005, Rink, Ghigo, Kalaidzidis and Zerial filmed single endosomes. Rab five was replaced by Rab seven while the cargo stayed in the same endosome. That supports maturation.
scenes.visual: Left panel Noctor 2001: a labelled radial glia cell budding a neuron over frames; right panel Rink 2005: one endosome blob with cargo dot, Rab5 ring fading as Rab7 ring grows; source tags under each.

scenes.tts: In 2015, Hines, Appel and colleagues filmed myelin wrapping in zebrafish. About 75% of wrapping attempts disappeared within 90 minutes. Wraps already formed on silenced axons retracted more often. Retraction is only seen in a movie. Keep one rule. A movie shows what those cells did, not what all cells do.
